title: Asking a Better Question
author: Jonathan Boymal
summary: Jonathan Boymal argues that the quality of a question shapes the quality of understanding, and that students will increasingly need to ask better questions in an age of instant answers. He draws on Socrates, Kuhn, Berlin and Rilke, and uses a student asking about the causes of World War I to show how a masterful teacher hears the question beneath the question. He distinguishes questions of fact, preference and judgment, and offers techniques such as Socratic probing, prior questions and scaffolded narrowing. He closes with three habits: slow the impulse to answer, trace the question to its source, and expand the frame.
points: A masterful teacher listens for the question beneath the question, turning a request for facts into an initiation into historical thinking.
Knowing whether a question is one of fact, preference or judgment determines how it should be pursued.
Socratic questioning, prior questions and scaffolded narrowing are concrete techniques for deepening an inquiry.
Instant answers from search engines and AI make it harder, and more important, to live with a question long enough for it to change you.
Three habits are offered: slow the impulse to answer, trace the question to its source, and expand the frame.
quotes: We tend to treat intelligence as the ability to produce answers. Yet discovery, change, and understanding, whether in science, art, or politics, almost always begin with a question.
The shape of your question, he knew, determines the shape of your understanding.

A competent teacher can supply that list. A masterful one hears the deeper questions beneath: How do complex historical events emerge from many causes at once? How do we distinguish between a trigger and an underlying tension?
Thomas Kuhn, in his history of science, showed that fields do not just advance by adding facts, but by shifting the very questions they ask.
The moment a question arises, we can throw it at a search engine or an AI and have an answer in seconds. Correct, perhaps. Transformative, rarely.
Questions of judgment require reasoning and weighing of evidence; they yield better or worse answers, not one final truth: How can society best address climate change?

First, slow the impulse to answer; let the question breathe. Second, trace it back to its source; ask where it comes from. Third, expand the frame; bring in perspectives and scenarios that open the inquiry beyond its starting point.
